sections.guidingQuestion: What makes a cell a unit of life rather than a molecule, tissue or virus?
sections.explanation:
Every living organism consists of one or more cells. A cell is the smallest organizational unit capable of coordinating life processes; many organisms consist of one cell, whereas multicellular organisms have cells organized into tissues and organs. A tissue is an association of specialized cells, not an alternative to cellular organization. Molecules such as DNA or proteins are vital components, but an isolated molecule cannot maintain the integrated processes of life.

Cell theory supports a deductive prediction: when scientists discover an unfamiliar living organism, they expect it to be made of cells. A freshwater Amoeba already demonstrates that one cell can perform many functions; a human muscle contains many cells organized in tissue. Viruses have genetic material and evolve, but lack independent cellular metabolism and are not counted as cellular organisms. The prediction is scientifically testable and must be reconsidered if strong contrary evidence emerges.

Evidence and prediction: imagine finding a microscopic green object in a pond. Seeing a green pigment is insufficient to call it an organism. Examine its boundary, whether it grows and reproduces under suitable conditions, and whether it carries out cellular activities. If several cells cooperate, distinguish each cell from the tissue or colony. An apparent contradiction to cell theory would need reproducible observations and careful exclusion of contamination and misidentification.
sections.revisionSummary: A newly described living organism should consist of one or more cells. Tissues are composed of cells; their integrated function arises from the activities of those cells.

sections.guidingQuestion: How can a microscope image become reliable quantitative evidence?
sections.explanation:
Prepare a thin temporary mount on a clean slide, use a suitable stain only when needed, and lower the coverslip carefully to reduce trapped air. Begin focusing at low power; use coarse adjustment cautiously, then fine focus, before moving to higher magnification. An eyepiece graticule must be calibrated for each objective using a stage micrometer. Record units, specimen context and technique, and take an image with a documented scale rather than assuming pixels correspond to a fixed physical length.

Magnification is image size divided by actual size, using the same units. If a 60 mm printed cell image represents an actual 30 µm cell, first convert 60 mm into 60,000 µm, then calculate 60,000/30 = ×2000. For a scale bar, calibrate image distance against a known specimen length: if 20 µm covers 40 mm on a print, a 10 µm bar must be 20 mm long on that same print. A digital display resize changes on-screen magnification, but a correctly embedded scale bar rescales with the image. Magnification is not resolution.

Practice calibration rather than trusting a microscope knob: if a stage micrometer shows 100 µm across 40 eyepiece-graticule divisions, one division represents 2.5 µm for that objective. A cell spanning 13 divisions is therefore 32.5 µm wide. Recalibrate when changing objective lenses. Record stain, specimen, lens combination and measurement uncertainty. When photographing, include a calibrated scale bar or enough metadata to create one; a ruler placed on the printed photo is not a physical specimen scale by itself.
sections.revisionSummary: Convert image and actual lengths to the same unit before dividing. Printed or screen magnification depends on display size; a correctly attached scale bar remains useful after proportional resizing.
sections.workedExample: A 45 mm image represents a 15 µm cell. 45 mm = 45,000 µm; magnification = 45,000/15 = ×3000. A 5 µm bar on that print would be 15 mm long.

sections.guidingQuestion: What improvements make structures visible beyond ordinary bright-field microscopy?
sections.explanation:
A light microscope can observe many living cells and, with fluorescent stains, can distinguish selected molecules or structures against a background. Immunofluorescence uses antibodies carrying fluorescent labels to localize target antigens; localization depends on antibody specificity, preparation and optical resolution. Conventional light microscopy is limited in spatial resolution by diffraction, so simply enlarging a blurry image does not reveal finer structures.

Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) reveals thin-section internal ultrastructure using transmitted electrons; scanning electron microscopy (SEM) emphasizes specimen surface topography. Electron methods generally need more complex preparation and often cannot examine living cells under conventional high-vacuum conditions. Freeze fracture splits frozen membranes to expose surfaces, while cryogenic electron microscopy rapidly vitrifies material to study structures with reduced crystallization damage. These methods answer different questions, not a universal ranking of 'best microscope'.

Choose by evidence required. To follow movement in a living protist, transmitted-light microscopy may be best. To find where an antibody binds inside a fixed cell, use appropriate immunofluorescent labeling with negative controls. TEM requires thin specimens and reveals internal membranes; SEM usually provides surface information. A freeze-fractured preparation exposes membrane faces, but freezing and etching can introduce artifacts. Cryo-EM vitrification minimizes ice-crystal damage and aids structural reconstruction. Report what was actually resolved, not what a familiar cartoon says should be present.
sections.revisionSummary: TEM can show internal ultrastructure when thin sections are prepared appropriately. The resolving power of the instrument and specimen preparation set what detail is distinguishable.
sections.workedExample: To localize a protein, select validated immunofluorescence. To inspect mitochondrial cristae, consider thin-section TEM. Explain how each preparation may introduce artifacts.

misconceptions.misconception: Higher magnification always produces more genuine detail.
misconceptions.correction: The resolving power of the instrument and specimen preparation set what detail is distinguishable.

sections.guidingQuestion: What common components support all cellular life?
sections.explanation:
Across living cells, hereditary DNA stores instructions, the cytoplasm provides a water-rich setting for reactions, and a lipid-based plasma membrane separates the cell interior from its environment. Ribosomes synthesize proteins in living cells. These are functional necessities: hereditary information can be copied and interpreted; an aqueous environment allows substances to interact; a boundary makes selective exchange and regulated chemistry possible.

What is shared does not mean every cell has a nucleus, chloroplast, mitochondrion or wall. In eukaryotes the DNA is usually enclosed by a nucleus, whereas prokaryotes lack a membrane-bounded nucleus. Many specialized mature cells may lose typical organelles, as in mammalian red blood cells; such exceptions do not invalidate common evolutionary cellular ancestry. Use the core features to recognize unity while comparing diversity.

Test which elements are common and which are typical. DNA can support inheritance because sequence information is copied; a plasma membrane permits cells to establish internal environments; ribosomes build proteins following encoded instructions. A wall is protective in many prokaryotes, plants and fungi, but its chemical construction varies and it is absent in animals. A nucleus is especially important in a typical eukaryotic organization but not universal among living cells. Build explanations using each structure's function rather than memorizing a universal organelle checklist.
sections.revisionSummary: A lipid plasma membrane encloses the aqueous cytoplasm. Bacteria and archaea lack nuclei; mature human erythrocytes also lack a nucleus.
sections.workedExample: A tiny cell has DNA, cytoplasm, a lipid membrane and ribosomes but no nucleus. The absence of a nucleus does not make it non-living.

sections.guidingQuestion: What can a Gram-positive bacterial cell do without a nucleus?
sections.explanation:
The syllabus reference model is a Gram-positive eubacterium such as Bacillus or Staphylococcus. A plasma membrane surrounds cytoplasm containing 70S ribosomes; genetic DNA is present in a nucleoid region, commonly as a circular chromosome not enclosed in a nuclear membrane. An external cell wall provides shape and mechanical protection. In Gram-positive bacteria the wall contains a thick peptidoglycan layer; wall and membrane must not be drawn as one structure.

Some bacteria possess extra surface features such as flagella, capsules or pili, but these are not universal and are not required components of the basic syllabus model. 'Naked DNA' here means DNA is not organized with eukaryotic histone-based chromatin in a nucleus; it does not imply DNA is unassociated with every protein. Prokaryotic cells are not just simplified eukaryotes; their organization and biochemical systems have distinct evolutionary histories.

Reason about layers: a Gram-positive bacterium has a thick peptidoglycan cell wall outside its plasma membrane, while the membrane controls traffic into its watery cytoplasm. Ribosomes are involved in protein synthesis even without a nucleus. The DNA loop is in the nucleoid, a region lacking a membrane boundary. Bacillus can be rod-shaped and Staphylococcus often forms spherical cells in clusters, although actual shapes vary. Never draw a flagellum or capsule as compulsory, and do not confuse Gram-positive peptidoglycan with a plant cellulose wall.
sections.revisionSummary: 70S ribosomes occur in the cytoplasm of the specified bacterial reference model. These features vary; do not add them to every bacterial diagram or require them for identification.
sections.workedExample: In a diagram of Bacillus, label an exterior wall, an interior plasma membrane, nucleoid DNA, aqueous cytoplasm and 70S ribosomes. Mark a capsule optional.

misconceptions.misconception: All bacteria have flagella, capsules and plasmids.
misconceptions.correction: These features vary; do not add them to every bacterial diagram or require them for identification.

sections.guidingQuestion: Why is compartmentalization a defining feature of most eukaryotic cells?
sections.explanation:
Eukaryotic cells have a plasma membrane enclosing a cytoplasm organized by internal membranes. A nucleus contains DNA associated with histone proteins, usually organized as chromosomes; its double nuclear envelope contains pores that regulate traffic. Cytosolic ribosomes are 80S. Mitochondria participate in aerobic respiration; rough endoplasmic reticulum carries ribosomes and supports synthesis of many secreted and membrane proteins; smooth ER participates in lipid synthesis and other functions. The Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts and packages cargo; vesicles and lysosomes support transport and degradation.

The cytoskeleton includes microtubules and actin microfilaments, which provide organization and help with movement and intracellular transport. Organelle occurrence varies among specialized eukaryotic cell types: chloroplasts are not found in animal cells, and a mature mammalian erythrocyte lacks its nucleus and mitochondria. Do not claim that all eukaryotes are identical or that organelles are floating in an unstructured fluid.

Trace a secreted protein as an organizational example: ribosomes associated with rough ER synthesize many proteins destined for secretion; membrane traffic can carry cargo to the Golgi apparatus for modification and sorting, then into vesicles that fuse with the plasma membrane. This illustrates why membranes organize specific tasks. A cytoskeleton also positions components and can assist intracellular movement. This sequence is a simplified model: not all proteins follow it, and ribosomes themselves lack surrounding membranes. Connect each compartment to a function rather than treating organelles as separate decorative icons.

sections.guidingQuestion: How can a unicellular organism perform functions that multicellular organisms divide among tissues?
sections.explanation:
A unicellular organism must perform homeostasis, metabolism, nutrition, movement when relevant, excretion, growth, responses to stimuli and reproduction within one integrated cellular system. Amoeba uses flexible extensions of its surface for movement and engulfment; Paramecium uses cilia and food vacuoles, while many green algae obtain energy by photosynthesis. These are distinct strategies, not a claim that every unicellular organism moves in the same way.

Homeostasis involves regulation of internal conditions; metabolism includes chemical reactions supplying materials and energy. Excretion removes metabolic waste rather than undigested food. A ciliated protist can swim toward suitable conditions and away from harmful ones: its response involves sensory and motor cellular processes without a nervous system. Division can produce new organisms because each resulting cell can function independently. The cell remains a coherent organism, not a miniature assemblage of organs.

Predict changes in a protist's behavior after a stimulus. In freshwater Paramecium, beating cilia supports movement; food particles can be brought into food vacuoles, while contractile vacuoles assist osmoregulation by expelling excess water. Reproduction by cell division creates two organisms when conditions permit. Each action requires coordinated molecular processes in the same cell. Metabolism includes both building and breaking down molecules, and homeostasis is regulation rather than literal constancy of every internal quantity.

sections.guidingQuestion: Which features genuinely distinguish major eukaryotic cell groups?
sections.explanation:
Many plant cells have cellulose-based walls, a large permanent sap vacuole and plastids, including chloroplasts in photosynthetic tissues. Fungal cells typically have chitin-rich walls and vacuoles, but do not have chloroplasts. Animal cells lack a rigid cell wall and commonly have small vesicular compartments; many possess centrioles, whereas centrioles are absent from many higher-plant cells. These features fit cellular functions, but individual specialized cells depart from familiar classroom drawings.

Cell walls are not interchangeable: cellulose, chitin and bacterial peptidoglycan differ in composition. Not every plant cell is photosynthetic: root cells usually lack chloroplasts. Cilia and flagella are present in selected eukaryotic cells or life-cycle stages rather than defining all members of a kingdom. Compare organism type, tissue, life stage and environmental function before declaring a feature universal.

Make a three-column evidence table before identifying an unfamiliar eukaryotic cell. Cellulose-rich walls and plastids suggest plant tissue; chitin-rich walls suggest fungi; a flexible cell edge without a wall may suggest animal tissue. Vacuoles and motile appendages can occur in more than one kingdom and vary with tissue or life stage. A potato storage cell may contain non-green plastids; a green leaf cell may contain chloroplasts. Compare several independent features, not one cartoon color or a single cell's roundness.

sections.guidingQuestion: What do nuclei reveal about unusual eukaryotic cellular organization?
sections.explanation:
Typical diagrams show one nucleus per eukaryotic cell, but this is a teaching model rather than a rule. Aseptate fungal hyphae can be continuous cytoplasmic tubes containing many nuclei without complete cross-walls. A skeletal muscle fibre is a very long multinucleate cell produced through fusion of precursor cells. Both cases show how one plasma-membrane-bounded living unit may contain multiple nuclei.

A mature mammalian red blood cell has expelled its nucleus, increasing space for haemoglobin and making it flexible, while a mature phloem sieve-tube element loses its nucleus and depends on an associated companion cell for many metabolic functions. A mature sieve element remains alive but is an unusually dependent cell. These are the four syllabus examples: compare them by number of nuclei and organization, rather than incorrectly assuming they represent four different kingdoms.

Use the four prescribed examples to challenge a one-nucleus stereotype. In a continuous aseptate fungal hypha, multiple nuclei share a cytoplasmic tube. Skeletal muscle fibres arise from fusion and use many nuclei across their large length. During maturation, human erythrocytes lose their nuclei, leaving more volume for haemoglobin; phloem sieve-tube elements lack nuclei and receive support from companion cells. Do not infer that nucleus-free mature cells are prokaryotes: their developmental history is eukaryotic.

sections.guidingQuestion: What evidence distinguishes structures in light and electron micrographs?
sections.explanation:
Interpret a micrograph by reading its scale, microscopy modality, specimen information and visible boundaries before applying any label. In light images, a clear cell wall, large vacuole and chloroplasts may support plant-cell classification; a bacterium may appear as a small featureless rod or sphere because its ribosomes cannot be individually resolved. In thin-section TEM, distinct membranes and electron-density patterns may support identifying the nucleus, mitochondrion, chloroplast, rough or smooth ER, Golgi stack, vacuole, ribosomes, chromosomes, nucleoid, microvilli or plasma membrane.

Look for clusters of parallel flattened cisternae with attached dark dots when proposing rough ER, stacks of curved smooth cisternae for Golgi, and double membrane plus internal cristae for a mitochondrion. Morphology overlaps and single 2D sections can be ambiguous; an identification is an evidence-based interpretation, not a guess from color. sections.guidingQuestion: Why do mitochondria and chloroplasts resemble bacteria? (HL)
sections.explanation:
The endosymbiotic model proposes that mitochondria and chloroplasts descend from bacteria that were retained within ancestral eukaryotic cells. Its strongest school-level evidence includes small 70S-type ribosomes, their own typically circular DNA and replication by division. Comparative genetic evidence further connects mitochondria to bacterial lineages and chloroplasts to cyanobacteria. Organelles are integrated into their host cells and many essential proteins are now nuclear encoded.

The official sequence describes an early nuclear-bearing, sexually reproducing unicellular common ancestor of eukaryotes, followed by mitochondrial endosymbiosis, with chloroplast endosymbiosis later in particular lineages. This is a historical reconstruction, not a directly recorded event; exact early ordering and the evolution of sex/nucleus remain active research topics. Distinguish evidence (genes, ribosomes, division) from inference (the particular ancestral cell interactions). The theory is compelling because it explains convergent lines of evidence and yields testable predictions.

Evaluate alternative explanations. Mitochondria and plastids maintain their own genetic material and division processes, and organellar ribosomes resemble bacterial counterparts. The bacterial affinity of numerous organelle genes provides an additional independent line of evidence. Modern mitochondria do not live freely in normal cells because evolutionary integration transferred or lost many genes. Students can identify the observable evidence and infer an ancestral bacterial partnership, but should not claim a photographed merger or insist that all proposed steps of early eukaryotic evolution are settled.

sections.guidingQuestion: How can cells sharing DNA develop different structures and functions? (HL)
sections.explanation:
Differentiation is the process by which an initially less-specialized cell acquires a characteristic pattern of structures and activities. In an organism's development, cells inherit broadly the same genome, but regulatory signals alter which genes are expressed. The resulting changes in protein production influence cytoskeleton, membranes, cell shape and physiology; cells with compatible functions can form tissues.

Environmental cues include concentration gradients of signalling molecules, interactions with adjacent cells and local extracellular conditions. A precursor cell responding to a positional signal may activate one regulatory program, while a nearby cell follows another; these differences can persist through later divisions. Not every mature specialized cell retains the same DNA complement—for instance, the mature human red blood cell has no nucleus. This distinction prepares for B2.3 without treating differentiation as mutation of the genome.

Differentiate cause from consequence. If two genetically similar early cells experience different neighbor signals, they may turn on different transcription factors, synthesize different proteins and acquire different cytoskeletal structures or membrane transporters. Tissue architecture then emerges from cells performing complementary roles. Cellular fate can become more restricted across development while many genetic sequences stay unchanged. Specialized maturation is not always reversible under normal circumstances; however, research reprogramming methods demonstrate that some differentiated states can be experimentally altered.

sections.guidingQuestion: Why does multicellularity evolve in more than one lineage? (HL)
sections.explanation:
Multicellularity evolved more than once in eukaryotic history. Animals and land plants are multicellular; many fungi and numerous algal groups also show multicellular forms. Multicellular individuals can become larger than typical solitary cells, creating ecological opportunities, and can partition work among cells that specialize in different functions. Coordination and transport become important constraints as body size increases.

The appearance of differentiated multicellular groups is best explained through heritable variation, ecological conditions and natural selection, not through cells consciously seeking complexity. Some lineages form colonies, others produce physically integrated tissues; these arrangements are not all equivalent. Comparative studies and evolutionary trees help infer independent origins. The actual steps differed among lineages and cannot be assumed from a single cartoon sequence.

questions.prompt: Two hypothetical calibration records show the same 100 µm interval on a stage micrometer. With lens A, it spans 40 eyepiece divisions and a cell spans 12 divisions. With lens B, the interval spans 80 divisions and the same cell spans 24 divisions. Calculate the µm/division at each objective, calculate the cell size using either calibration, and explain why reusing lens A's calibration for lens B would be invalid. [5 marks]
questions.answer: Lens A: 100/40 = 2.5 µm per graticule division, giving 12 × 2.5 = 30 µm. Lens B: 100/80 = 1.25 µm per division, giving 24 × 1.25 = 30 µm. Each objective maps a different specimen distance to one eyepiece division; using the wrong lens calibration for lens B would incorrectly give 24 × 2.5 = 60 µm.
markingPoints: Lens A calibration calculated as 2.5 µm per eyepiece division.
Lens B calibration calculated as 1.25 µm per eyepiece division.
Correct specimen size of 30 µm obtained using lens A.
Correct specimen size of 30 µm obtained using lens B.
Explains objective-dependent calibration and/or shows the invalid 60 µm estimate if lens A calibration were reused.

questions.prompt: An investigator observes a long eukaryotic structure containing several nuclei and a second mature plant transport cell with no nucleus. Give one syllabus example of each and explain how the two structures remain consistent with cell theory even though they differ from common cell diagrams. [4 marks]
questions.answer: A multinucleate eukaryotic example is an aseptate fungal hypha or a skeletal muscle fibre. The anucleate mature plant transport element is a phloem sieve-tube element. The multinucleate examples are living membrane-bounded cytoplasmic structures with many nuclei; mature sieve elements are specialized eukaryotic cells that lose their nucleus and are sustained by companion cells. Typical one-nucleus diagrams are models, not universal laws.
markingPoints: Identifies aseptate fungal hypha or skeletal muscle fibre as a multinucleate eukaryotic example.
Explains the continuous hyphal cytoplasm or muscle precursor fusion supporting more than one nucleus.
Identifies the anucleate plant example as mature phloem sieve-tube element.
Explains dependence on companion cells and/or why a differentiated anucleate eukaryotic element is not prokaryotic.
